prompt: The writer argues chiefly that
passage:
Pye and Son of Marram print 1691 on their wrappers, on the fascia over the shop, and on the fourth page of the town's visitor brochure, where the business is called the oldest bakery in England still working from one address. I have spent two winters on that claim. I can say what it rests on, and I can say what it is worth.

It rests on two things, and both of them are real. A date-stone cut with the year 1691 is set in the wall of the yard behind the shop, four feet above the ground and directly over the oven's stoke-hole. And a deed of 1742 conveys the bakehouse in Fore Street to one Josiah Pye, who is certainly an ancestor of the family that bakes there now.

The stone was not cut for that wall. Marram's Independent chapel was pulled down in 1889, and the builder who took the contract, Henry Flack, kept a day-book which is in the county office and which anybody may call up. Under 4 September he entered the carriage of the datestone and two corbels from the chapel yard to Fore Street, and charged three shillings for setting the first of them. The chapel was built in 1691. The stone has been telling the truth about the chapel for three hundred years, and telling it, since 1889, on the wrong wall.

The deed is honest too, and it is about a different building. Fore Street was renumbered in 1866, when the four cottages at the top were taken down and the street was counted from the church end instead of the bridge end. The bakehouse conveyed in 1742 stood at what is now number 31, which is the chemist's; the deed's own boundaries name the smithy on one side and the churchyard wall on the other, and neither of those has ever touched the present shop, which stands sixty yards off and on the opposite side.

What is true is better than what is printed, and it is out in the yard. The oven is brick-lined, and the bricks are the long thin sort made before the tax on brick sizes changed the trade's habits after 1803. The firm's own coal accounts begin in 1799, and they open with a repair to the oven, not with its building. Nobody else in this county has a working oven that can be shown to be as old. That is a distinction, it is defensible, and it is the claim they ought to be making.

I have no quarrel with the Pyes. The family did not invent the date; a brochure writer handed it to them in 1974 and they have been living up to it ever since, and I do not think it is a baker's business to audit a brochure. The wrapper is another matter. It is printed by the thousand, it is wrong, and it is the only thing about that shop most people will ever read. Drop the line, put the oven in its place, and they lose nothing but a sentence.
